# F3A downgrades

These descriptions are generated from the Tuning package of FCScore and describe what FCScore measures for each downgrade. See the [downgrade reference](index.md) for how to read them.

> - [FAI CIAM F3A 2026 Sporting Code](https://www.fai.org/sites/default/files/document/file/SC4_volume_CIAM%20F3A%202026.pdf)

## Intra-element downgrades

### Constant Speed {#speed}

`speed`

Checks that the aircraft keeps a constant speed over the ground through the lines and loops of the manoeuvre, including climbs and descents. The variation of speed about its mean over a run of consecutive lines and loops is charged once for the whole run, whether the aircraft speeds up or slows down, and the downgrade is shared across the elements of the run. Small speed changes are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    F3A asks for a constant flying speed through all the components of a manoeuvre, including climbing and descending sections, and defines it as three-dimensional velocity rather than airspeed. The aircraft should therefore look as though it is travelling at the same pace on the up-lines, the down-lines and the loops, without surging on the way down or running out of speed over the top.

    FCScore measures the speed of the aircraft's centre of gravity over lines and loops; spins and stall turns, and the lines and loops directly next to them, are left out. The spread of the speed about its mean, as a fraction of the mean speed, is charged in proportion to its size, so a steady slow-down is charged as well as a sudden burst of power. Consecutive lines and loops are assessed as one continuous run, so a change that straddles an element boundary is only counted once and the downgrade is shared across the elements of the run. The rulebook limits this criterion to significant differences and about one point, so the scale is deliberately gentle.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small change is charged. Speed changes are easiest to see when the aircraft is crossing the judge's view and harder when it is travelling towards or away from the judge, and they are harder to judge high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales speed errors. Large changes are counted in full.

> The model aircraft shall maintain a constant flight speed throughout the various manoeuvre components; for example, in climbing and descending sections. For significant differences up to one point is subtracted.
>
> [5B.9](#rb-speed)

> Constant Flying Speed (three-dimensional velocity—not airspeed);
>
> [5B.3](#rb-speed.ground_speed)

### Line Heading Drift {#track_z}

`track_z`

Checks that the flight path of each line stays on the template heading, with no sideways drift or turning away. Only growth in the heading error is charged, so a correction back towards the line is free and an error carried in from the previous element is not charged again. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Every line must be flown with its flight path pointing exactly where the manoeuvre requires, wind corrected so that the path over the ground is straight. F3A judges the flight path (the trajectory of the centre of gravity) rather than the direction the nose points, so crabbing into a crosswind is fine but the path itself must not wander. The guide also asks that lines are judged more critically than yaw or roll deviations.

    FCScore compares the direction of the aircraft's velocity with the template line and measures the sideways (heading) angle between them, for lines that sit between other elements of the manoeuvre, apart from lines next to spins and stall turns. Each increase in the absolute error is charged and each decrease is free, so a drift that builds up costs points while correcting back does not, and an error already present at the start of the line is not charged a second time. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Because every separate increase is charged, small wobbles add up with time, so the same flying in a bigger manoeuvre, which takes longer at the same speed, would collect more of them. To keep the size of the manoeuvre from counting against the pilot, this downgrade is multiplied by (reference duration / flown duration) to the power 0.75, limited to between 0.7 and 1.4. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The flight path of a model aircraft is the trajectory of its centre of gravity. The attitude is the direction of the fuselage centre-line in relation to the flight path. If not otherwise stated, all judging is based on flight path.
>
> [5B.6](#rb-general.flight_path)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Line Pitch Drift {#track_y}

`track_y`

Checks that the flight path of each line stays at the template pitch, with no climbing, sinking or leaning away from the intended line. Only growth in the pitch error is charged, so a correction back towards the line is free and an error carried in from the previous element is not charged again. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Every line must be flown with its flight path at exactly the angle the manoeuvre requires: level on a horizontal line, truly vertical on an up- or down-line. F3A judges the flight path rather than the nose attitude, and requires wind correction, so a vertical line flown into wind must still go straight up even though the nose is tilted. The guide asks that lines are judged more critically than yaw or roll deviations.

    FCScore compares the direction of the aircraft's velocity with the template line and measures the angle between them in the pitch direction of the line (climbing or sinking on a horizontal line, leaning forwards or backwards on a vertical one), for lines that sit between other elements of the manoeuvre, apart from lines next to spins and stall turns. Each increase in the absolute error is charged and each decrease is free, so a drift that builds up costs points while correcting back does not, and an error already present at the start of the line is not charged again. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The flight path of a model aircraft is the trajectory of its centre of gravity. The attitude is the direction of the fuselage centre-line in relation to the flight path. If not otherwise stated, all judging is based on flight path.
>

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.

### Entry Line Heading {#entry_track_z}

`entry_track_z`

Checks the heading of the flight path at the end of the entry line. The full angle between the flight path and the template heading is charged at that point, so the line must settle on the correct heading before the manoeuvre starts. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    A manoeuvre must be entered with straight and level flight of recognisable length, and F3A judges that flight on its flight path. By the end of the entry line the aircraft should be tracking exactly along the heading the manoeuvre starts from, with no residual turn left over from the previous manoeuvre or a late correction.

    FCScore takes the last point of the entry line, the first element of the manoeuvre, and charges the whole angle between the direction of travel and the template heading there. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier in the manoeuvre has been charged yet. An error that has been corrected before the end of the line is not charged, but one that is still present as the first element begins is. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The flight path of a model aircraft is used to judge the shape of all manoeuvres, and manoeuvres must be entered and exited with straight and level upright or inverted flight of recognisable length.
>
> [5B.2](#rb-lines.level_flight)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Loop Plane Drift {#axial_track}

`axial_track`

Checks that the flight path of each loop stays in the plane of the loop, without drifting towards or away from the judge. Only growth in the out-of-plane angle is charged, so correcting back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A loop must be flown entirely in its own plane, which for a vertical loop means it must not drift closer to or further from the judges. Minor drift is penalised and severe drift more heavily, and because F3A requires wind correction the pilot must hold the loop in the plane despite a crosswind.

    FCScore measures the angle between the direction of travel and the plane of the loop, that is, the component of the flight path along the loop's axis. Each increase in that angle is charged and each decrease is free, so a drift that builds up costs points but a correction back towards the plane does not. The error at the start of a loop is not charged again if it was already charged on the previous element. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Because every separate increase is charged, small wobbles add up with time, so the same flying in a bigger manoeuvre, which takes longer at the same speed, would collect more of them. To keep the size of the manoeuvre from counting against the pilot, this downgrade is multiplied by (reference duration / flown duration) to the power 0.75, limited to between 0.7 and 1.4. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> A loop must have by definition, a constant radius, and must be performed in the vertical plane throughout. It is entered and exited by a well-defined line which, for a complete loop, is horizontal. For a part-loop, however, such lines may be in any other plane of flight as required by the particular manoeuvre.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.definition)

> If the loop is not performed entirely in the vertical plane ie it drifts closer or further from the judges, minor drift must be downgraded by 0.5 point, while more severe drift must be downgraded more.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.plane)

### Loop Exit Angle {#radial_track}

`radial_track`

Checks that the flight path at the end of each loop points in the intended direction within the plane of the loop, so the loop has not been over- or under-flown. The full angle error at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    A loop or part-loop is exited with a well-defined line in the direction the manoeuvre requires: horizontal for a complete loop, or the vertical or 45° line that follows for a part-loop. The arc should therefore finish at exactly the right angle, with no extra or missing degrees.

    FCScore takes the last point of each loop and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the template direction, measured within the plane of the loop. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over-rotated or under-rotated arc is charged here once; the line that follows is then only charged for further changes, so the same error is not charged twice. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> A loop must have by definition, a constant radius, and must be performed in the vertical plane throughout. It is entered and exited by a well-defined line which, for a complete loop, is horizontal. For a part-loop, however, such lines may be in any other plane of flight as required by the particular manoeuvre.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.definition)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>

### Spin Approach Heading {#prespin_initial_track_z}

`prespin_initial_track_z`

Checks the heading of the flight path at the start of the last five seconds of the line leading into a spin. The full angle error there is charged, so the aircraft must be on the correct heading as it begins to slow for the stall. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    A spin is entered from a horizontal line with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed falls. Before the aircraft is close to the stall it should be tracking exactly along the entry heading, because F3A still judges the approach on its flight path.

    FCScore takes the final five seconds of the entry line before a spin and charges the whole heading error between the flight path and the template at the first point of that window. It is an absolute measure at that point because it is where the aircraft begins to approach the stall. Changes after that point are charged separately. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The entry is flown in a horizontal flight path with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed decreases. Drift of the model aircraft from the flight path at this point should not be downgraded, since it is in a near-stalled condition. However, severe yawing during the near-stalled condition, should be downgraded by 1 point per 15 degrees. A climbing flight path just prior to the spin must be downgraded, using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.entry)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Climb Before Spin {#prespin_track_y}

`prespin_track_y`

Checks that the flight path stays level in the last five seconds before a spin. Any growth in the pitch error, a climb or a sink, is charged, and correcting back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    The entry to a spin is flown on a horizontal flight path while the nose rises as the speed decays. The rulebook specifically says a climbing flight path just before the spin must be downgraded with the one point per 15° rule, so the aircraft should not be zoomed up into the stall.

    FCScore looks at the pitch direction of the flight path over the last five seconds of the entry line and charges each increase in the absolute pitch error, so a climb (or a sink) that develops as the aircraft slows is charged in proportion to its size. A decrease in the error is free. The error at the start of the window is charged once, at that point. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The entry is flown in a horizontal flight path with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed decreases. Drift of the model aircraft from the flight path at this point should not be downgraded, since it is in a near-stalled condition. However, severe yawing during the near-stalled condition, should be downgraded by 1 point per 15 degrees. A climbing flight path just prior to the spin must be downgraded, using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.entry)

### Upwind Turn Before Spin {#prespin_upwind_track}

`prespin_upwind_track`

Checks that the flight path does not turn towards the wind in the last five seconds before a spin. Only turning into wind is charged; drift downwind is ignored as part of the near-stalled condition. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Near the stall the aircraft is allowed to drift off its flight path, because it is in a near-stalled condition and wind has more effect. The rulebook only asks for downgrades when the aircraft is deliberately yawed or steered, so the approach should stay straight apart from natural downwind drift.

    FCScore measures the horizontal-plane angle between the flight path and the template over the last five seconds of the entry line, but counts it only where the path turns towards the upwind direction; errors that point downwind are set to zero. Each increase in that upwind angle is charged and each decrease is free. The wind direction is estimated from the aircraft's own data. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The entry is flown in a horizontal flight path with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed decreases. Drift of the model aircraft from the flight path at this point should not be downgraded, since it is in a near-stalled condition. However, severe yawing during the near-stalled condition, should be downgraded by 1 point per 15 degrees. A climbing flight path just prior to the spin must be downgraded, using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.entry)

### Excessive Yaw Before Spin {#prespin_excessive_yaw}

`prespin_excessive_yaw`

Checks that the nose is not yawed far towards the wind in the last five seconds before a spin. Only the largest upwind yaw beyond 15° is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Drift near the stall is not downgraded, but F3A does downgrade severe yawing in the near-stalled condition at one point per 15°. The nose should stay close to the line of flight as the aircraft slows into the stall.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage axis relative to the template in the horizontal plane over the last five seconds of the entry line, counting only yaw towards the upwind direction. A single downgrade is given for the largest angle beyond 15°, in proportion to how far beyond. This is a measure of the nose attitude rather than the flight path.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The entry is flown in a horizontal flight path with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed decreases. Drift of the model aircraft from the flight path at this point should not be downgraded, since it is in a near-stalled condition. However, severe yawing during the near-stalled condition, should be downgraded by 1 point per 15 degrees. A climbing flight path just prior to the spin must be downgraded, using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>

### Entry Wings Level {#entry_roll}

`entry_roll`

Checks that the wings are level (or at the template roll attitude) at the end of the entry line. The full roll angle error is charged at that point. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A manoeuvre must be entered from straight and level upright or inverted flight, so by the end of the entry line the wings should be level with no bank carried over from the previous manoeuvre. F3A downgrades roll deviations at about one point per 15°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the entry line, the first element of the manoeuvre, and charges the whole difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier in the manoeuvre has been charged. A bank that has been removed before the end of the line is not charged, but one that is still present when the first element begins is. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The flight path of a model aircraft is used to judge the shape of all manoeuvres, and manoeuvres must be entered and exited with straight and level upright or inverted flight of recognisable length.
>
> [5B.2](#rb-lines.level_flight)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Unintended Roll Angle {#roll}

`roll`

Checks that the wings hold their correct attitude through lines, loops and stall turns that contain no roll. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Where a manoeuvre has no roll, the wings should stay exactly where the template puts them, level on a line and in the plane of the loop on a loop, with no wing drop or wobble. F3A downgrades roll deviations at one point per 15°, and judges lines more critically than roll.

    FCScore measures the aircraft's roll angle about its direction of travel relative to the template, on lines, loops and stall turns that do not contain a roll, other than the entry line. Each increase in the absolute roll error is charged and each decrease is free, so a wing drop costs points but picking the wing back up does not, and an angle already present at the start of the element is not charged again. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Because every separate increase is charged, small wobbles add up with time, so the same flying in a bigger manoeuvre, which takes longer at the same speed, would collect more of them. To keep the size of the manoeuvre from counting against the pilot, this downgrade is multiplied by (reference duration / flown duration) to the power 0.75, limited to between 0.7 and 1.4. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Rotation Amount {#roll_amount}

`roll_amount`

Checks that a roll, snap or spin finishes at the planned attitude. At the point of maximum rotation, the roll attitude is compared with the planned attitude and the difference is charged once, so both over- and under-rotation count. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Every roll and part-roll must start and stop crisply at the angle the manoeuvre defines, and a spin stops at the defined number of turns, aligned parallel to the flight line. F3A downgrades angle errors at one point per 15°, and says a roll that slows towards the end of its rotation or a spin that is unloaded early is penalised with that rule.

    FCScore finds the point of maximum rotation in each rotating element (roll, snap or spin) and compares the aircraft's roll attitude there with the planned attitude. It assesses the final attitude, not the total number of degrees rolled, although it tracks the rotation continuously (allowing for the angle wrapping round at 180°) so that a roll that overshoots by a full turn is not mistaken for a correct one. Over-rotation and under-rotation are charged equally, as a single absolute error at that point, and any movement after the maximum, such as rolling back, is charged separately. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

> The start and stop of the rotation must be crisp and well-defined. If a start or stop is badly defined, 0.5 or more points are to be subtracted for each.
>
> [5B.8.5 c)](#rb-rolls.start_stop)

> After the defined number of turns, the stop of rotation is judged in the same manner as for a roll, downgraded 1 point per 15 degree deviation of heading. The spin rotation should stop parallel to the flight line. “Unloading”, or stopping the spin rotation early and then applying only aileron to roll the model aircraft to the desired attitude, should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.stop)

### Roll Rebound {#rebound}

`rebound`

Checks that a roll stays where it stopped. After the maximum rotation, any growth in the roll error, such as bouncing back past the target or wobbling, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The stop of a roll must be crisp and well defined: the wings should arrive at the final angle and stay there, with no bounce or oscillation afterwards.

    FCScore looks at the part of each rotating element after the point of maximum rotation and charges each increase in the absolute roll error there. An over-rotation is charged once, at the point of maximum rotation, so rolling back from it is not charged again, but rolling back past the target, or rocking the wings, creates a new increase that is charged. A decrease in the error is free. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The start and stop of the rotation must be crisp and well-defined. If a start or stop is badly defined, 0.5 or more points are to be subtracted for each.
>
> [5B.8.5 c)](#rb-rolls.start_stop)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Rolling Loop Integration {#roll_integration}

`roll_integration`

Checks that the roll in a rolling loop progresses in step with the loop. The flight path error compared with the position expected for the current roll angle is charged whenever it grows. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: when the aircraft is viewed from above or below, along the line of sight, high or wide in the box, or at awkward angles, and for short loops or rolls.

??? note "Details"

    When a roll is integrated into a loop, the flight path should be smooth and continuous with constant radius, and the roll should be spread evenly around the loop so that the roll and the loop advance together. Quick-rolling is downgraded at one point per 15°.

    FCScore compares how far round the loop the aircraft actually is with how far round it should be for the proportion of the roll completed, and measures the angle between the two. Each increase in that angle is charged and each decrease is free, so rolling too early or too late, and flying part of the roll on a straight line, creates errors that are charged in proportion to their size. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Because every separate increase is charged, small wobbles add up with time, so the same flying in a bigger manoeuvre, which takes longer at the same speed, would collect more of them. To keep the size of the manoeuvre from counting against the pilot, this downgrade is multiplied by (reference duration / flown duration) to the power 0.75, limited to between 0.7 and 1.4. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. It combines how visible the flight path error is (easier across the judge's line of sight than along it) with how visible the roll is (easier side-on than looking at the top or underside), and it falls for aircraft high in the box or far off to one side and for awkward line and bank angles. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of loop and the amount of roll flown, so a short loop or a short roll counts for less.

> Flight paths of continuous rolls or part-rolls that are integrated with loops or horizontal circles should be smooth, continuous, and of constant radius. Where an integrated roll is required, quick-rolling should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.10](#rb-rolls.integration)

### Roll Rate Consistency {#roll_rate}

`roll_rate`

Checks that the roll rate is constant through each roll. The size of the variation in roll rate, compared with the average, is charged once for the roll. Small variations are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, and for short part-rolls that give less to judge.

??? note "Details"

    The roll rate must be constant: minor variations are penalised by 0.5 point and more severe variations by a point or more, and slowing down or speeding up towards the end of a roll is penalised with the one point per 15° rule.

    FCScore measures the roll rate throughout each roll and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average (the standard deviation divided by the mean). A steady roll scores zero, whatever its rate. The more the rate varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting also grows with the amount of roll flown: a full roll or more counts fully, a half roll counts about half, because short rolls give the judge less to assess. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors.

> The roll-rate must be constant. Minor variations in roll-rate must be downgraded by 0.5 point, while more severe variations must receive a downgrade of 1 or more points. Slowing down (or speeding up) the roll-rate towards the end of a roll must be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.5 b)](#rb-rolls.rate)

### Roll Pauses {#roll_excitation}

`roll_excitation`

Checks that the roll does not stop partway. The share of the roll for which the roll rate is close to zero, or in the wrong direction, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    A roll or part-roll should rotate continuously from a crisp start to a crisp stop. A pause in the middle of a roll breaks the constant roll rate that F3A requires.

    FCScore counts the time during each roll in which the roll rate is effectively zero or reversed. A roll rate below about 1.5° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 3° per second counts as moving, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the roll's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief hesitation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> The roll-rate must be constant. Minor variations in roll-rate must be downgraded by 0.5 point, while more severe variations must receive a downgrade of 1 or more points. Slowing down (or speeding up) the roll-rate towards the end of a roll must be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.5 b)](#rb-rolls.rate)

> The start and stop of the rotation must be crisp and well-defined. If a start or stop is badly defined, 0.5 or more points are to be subtracted for each.
>
> [5B.8.5 c)](#rb-rolls.start_stop)

### Loop Roundness {#radius}

`radius`

Checks that each loop is round, with a constant radius throughout. The variation of the radius within the loop, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, high or wide in the box, and part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    A loop must by definition have a constant radius and be flown in one plane, so it should look perfectly round, not egg-shaped, squared off or tighter in one quadrant than the rest.

    FCScore fits a circle to the flown path of the loop in the plane of the loop and measures how much the aircraft's distance from the fitted centre varies, as a fraction of the average radius. A perfectly round loop scores zero, whatever its size, and the more the radius varies the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Shape errors are easiest to see when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where distortions are hidden. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter. Large errors are counted in full.

> A loop must have by definition, a constant radius, and must be performed in the vertical plane throughout. It is entered and exited by a well-defined line which, for a complete loop, is horizontal. For a part-loop, however, such lines may be in any other plane of flight as required by the particular manoeuvre.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.definition)

### Flat Spots in Loops {#radius_excitation}

`radius_excitation`

Checks that the loop has no straight sections. The share of the loop for which the flight path is effectively straight is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Every loop or part-loop must be flown without interruption to the circular flight path, and each segmentation, such as a squared-off corner or a flat spot, is downgraded by 0.5 point or more.

    FCScore watches the curvature of the flight path throughout the loop and counts the time during which it is effectively straight, or curving the wrong way. A local radius of about 500 m or more counts as fully flat and about 250 m or less counts as curved, with values in between counting partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the loop's duration that is flat, so a long flat spot costs more than a brief one.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> Every loop or part-loop must be performed without interruption to the circular flight path. Every segmentation must be downgraded by 0.5 or more points.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.segmentation)

### Loop Rate of Turn {#curvature}

`curvature`

Checks that the loop keeps a steady rate of turn for its speed. The variation in the loop's curvature, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    A loop must have a constant radius, which means the aircraft has to turn at a steady rate for its speed. The loop should neither tighten nor open up as it goes round, including at the top where the aircraft is slowest.

    FCScore measures the rate of turn divided by the speed of travel (the curvature, which is one over the radius) throughout the loop and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. Because it is based on how quickly the aircraft is turning for its speed, it picks up a tightening or opening of the loop before the flight path has moved far. The more the curvature varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> A loop must have by definition, a constant radius, and must be performed in the vertical plane throughout. It is entered and exited by a well-defined line which, for a complete loop, is horizontal. For a part-loop, however, such lines may be in any other plane of flight as required by the particular manoeuvre.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.definition)

### Spin Rotation Axis {#spin_rotation_axis}

`spin_rotation_axis`

Checks that the spin is a stalled autorotation rather than an aileron-type roll. The time the aircraft rotates about an axis too close to its own fuselage line, below 15°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    To spin, the model must be stalled, and F3A zeroes a spin that is entered by a snap or spiral dive and severely downgrades one that returns to an unstalled condition. In a stalled spin the aircraft rotates about a steep axis while the fuselage is pitched down, so the rotation does not simply turn the aircraft about its own length.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is actually rotating about, from 15° after the break to 45° before the end of the rotation. Any period in which that angle is below 15° looks more like a roll about the fuselage than a spin and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and for how large a share of the spin. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting a stalled rotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> If the model aircraft does not stall or if the model aircraft is snap-rolled or spiral-dived into the spin, the manoeuvre is zeroed.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.stalled)

> Different models spin in different attitudes, and the attitude is not to be taken into consideration, as long as the model aircraft is stalled. Any reversals in direction must be immediate, and if the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the spin, the manoeuvre is severely downgraded.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.rotation)

### Spin Nose Drop {#drop_pitch_rate}

`drop_pitch_rate`

Checks that the nose drops decisively as the aircraft stalls into the spin. Time spent dropping slower than 10° per second in the first 15° of rotation is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: with the aircraft high or wide in the box, or directly above the judge.

??? note "Details"

    As the model stalls the nose drops and, at the same time, the wing drops in the direction of the spin. A model that slides into the spin, reluctant to drop, is downgraded with the one point per 15° rule.

    FCScore measures the nose-down pitch rate from the start of the spin until the first 15° of rotation has been completed. Any period in which it is below 10° per second is charged, according to how far below that rate it is and for how large a share of that window. The 10° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite nose drop, not a number from the rules. It applies to spin elements that follow a non-spin element.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The nose drop is harder to see when the aircraft is directly above the judge, and when it is high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error. Large errors are counted in full.

> The nose then drops as the model aircraft stalls. Simultaneously as the nose drops, the wing also drops in the direction of the spin.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.stall_break)

> If the model aircraft slides into the spin (is loath to spin), the manoeuvre must be downgraded by using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.slide_in)

### Spin Rotation Hesitation {#spin_excitation}

`spin_excitation`

Checks that the spin keeps rotating. The share of the spin for which the rotation rate is very low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Once the spin has started, rotation must continue to the end of the defined turns. Stopping the rotation early and finishing with ailerons, or hesitating in the middle, is downgraded, and a model that returns to an unstalled condition during the spin is severely downgraded.

    FCScore counts the time in each spin during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is close to zero or reversed. A rate below about 9° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 17° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the spin's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief hesitation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Different models spin in different attitudes, and the attitude is not to be taken into consideration, as long as the model aircraft is stalled. Any reversals in direction must be immediate, and if the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the spin, the manoeuvre is severely downgraded.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.rotation)

> After the defined number of turns, the stop of rotation is judged in the same manner as for a roll, downgraded 1 point per 15 degree deviation of heading. The spin rotation should stop parallel to the flight line. “Unloading”, or stopping the spin rotation early and then applying only aileron to roll the model aircraft to the desired attitude, should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.stop)

### Spin Exit Pitch Track {#spin_exit_y_track}

`spin_exit_y_track`

Checks that the flight path is vertical down at the end of the spin. The full pitch error between the flight path and the template downline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the rotation stops a vertical downward line of visible length must be held, and the stop is judged in the same way as for a roll, at about one point per 15°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin element and charges the whole angle between the direction the aircraft is travelling and the template downline, in the pitch direction. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction of travel (the flight path). The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> A vertical downward line of visible length must be held after the rotation stops. The pull- or push-out is judged like a part-loop and if followed by a part-roll, should be separated by a well-defined line of straight flight.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.exit)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Spin Exit Sideways Track {#spin_exit_z_track}

`spin_exit_z_track`

Checks that the flight path is not drifting sideways at the end of the spin. The full sideways error between the flight path and the template downline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the rotation stops a vertical downward line of visible length must be held, and the spin should stop parallel to the flight line. Heading deviations at the stop are downgraded at about one point per 15°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin element and charges the whole angle between the direction the aircraft is travelling and the template downline, in the sideways direction of the line's reference frame. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction of travel (the flight path). The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> A vertical downward line of visible length must be held after the rotation stops. The pull- or push-out is judged like a part-loop and if followed by a part-roll, should be separated by a well-defined line of straight flight.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.exit)

> After the defined number of turns, the stop of rotation is judged in the same manner as for a roll, downgraded 1 point per 15 degree deviation of heading. The spin rotation should stop parallel to the flight line. “Unloading”, or stopping the spin rotation early and then applying only aileron to roll the model aircraft to the desired attitude, should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.12](#rb-spins.stop)

### Snap Rotation Axis {#snap_rotation_axis}

`snap_rotation_axis`

Checks that the snap is a stalled autorotation rather than an axial roll. The time the aircraft rotates about an axis too close to its fuselage line, below 7.5°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A snap-roll is a rapid auto-rotative roll in a stalled attitude, and axial rolls disguised as snap-rolls must be severely downgraded. In a real snap the aircraft pitches and yaws away from its flight path, so its rotation is not simply a spin about its own fuselage line.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the start of the rotation to 90° before its end. Any period in which that angle is below 7.5° looks like an axial roll and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and for how large a share of the snap. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting a stalled rotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> If the stall-break does not occur and the model aircraft barrel-rolls around, the manoeuvre must be severely downgraded (more than 5 points). Similarly, axial rolls disguised as snap-rolls must be severely downgraded (more than 5 points).
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.axial_disguise)

> If the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the snap-roll, the manoeuvre is downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.unstalled)

### Snap Pitch Break {#break_pitch_rate}

`break_pitch_rate`

Checks that the snap starts with a clear pitch break. If the peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation never reaches 35° per second, the shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the start of a snap-roll the fuselage must show a definite stall-break and attitude separation from the flight path before the rotation starts. If there is no break and the model barrel-rolls around, the manoeuvre must be severely downgraded.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and takes its largest absolute value. If that peak never reaches 35° per second the shortfall is charged, and any peak above it is not. The 35° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite break, not a number from the rules, and only the peak counts.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> At the start of a snap-roll, the fuselage attitude must show a definite stall-break and attitude separation from the flight path, before the rotation is started, since the model aircraft is supposed to be in a stalled condition throughout the snap-roll.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.stall_break)

### Snap Rotation Rate {#snap_rate}

`snap_rate`

Checks that the snap rotates rapidly. Time spent rotating slower than 360° per second through the middle of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see, which is when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft.

??? note "Details"

    A snap-roll is defined as a rapid auto-rotative roll in a stalled attitude, so it should look clearly faster and more violent than an axial roll.

    FCScore measures the rotation rate of the snap from 25° after the start to 90° before the end, and charges any period in which it is below 360° per second in either direction, according to how far below and for how much of that window. The rulebook does not give a minimum rate; the 360° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a rapid rotation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Rotation rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside; the only visibility factor is this viewing angle. Large errors are counted in full.

> A snap-roll is a rapid auto-rotative roll where the model aircraft is in a stalled attitude, with a continuous high angle of attack.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.definition)

### Snap Rotation Hesitation {#snap_excitation}

`snap_excitation`

Checks that the snap keeps rotating. The share of the snap for which the rotation rate is low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    A snap-roll must remain stalled and auto-rotating throughout. If the model returns to an unstalled condition, or stops rotating part way, it is downgraded with the one point per 15° rule.

    FCScore counts the time in each snap during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is low. A rate below about 30° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 57° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the snap's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> If the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the snap-roll, the manoeuvre is downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.unstalled)

### Snap Exit Pitch {#snap_exit_y_track}

`snap_exit_y_track`

Checks that the snap does not leave the flight path pointing differently in pitch. Only an increase in the pitch error between the start and the end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Snap-rolls are judged like axial rolls as far as the constant flight path throughout the roll is concerned, so the aircraft should come out of the snap on the same line it went in on.

    FCScore compares the flight path direction with the template at the first and last points of the snap, in the pitch direction, and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and the error present before the snap is not charged again. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Snap-rolls are judged in the same way as axial rolls as far as the constant flight path throughout the snap-roll, the start and stop of the rotation, and the roll direction is concerned.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.geometry)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Snap Exit Heading {#snap_exit_z_track}

`snap_exit_z_track`

Checks that the snap does not leave the flight path pointing differently sideways. Only an increase in the heading error between the start and the end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Snap-rolls are judged like axial rolls as far as the constant flight path throughout the roll is concerned, so the aircraft should come out of the snap on the same line it went in on.

    FCScore compares the flight path direction with the template at the first and last points of the snap, in the sideways direction, and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and the error present before the snap is not charged again. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Snap-rolls are judged in the same way as axial rolls as far as the constant flight path throughout the snap-roll, the start and stop of the rotation, and the roll direction is concerned.
>
> [5B.8.7](#rb-snap_rolls.geometry)

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.
>
> [5B.8.2](#rb-general.fifteen_degrees)

### Stall Turn Pivot Width {#width}

`width`

Checks that the aircraft pivots in place at the top of a stall turn. The sideways distance travelled in the direction of the turn beyond 2 m is charged, ignoring downwind drift. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a stall turn the aircraft comes to a stop in forward movement and must pivot about its centre of gravity in the yaw axis. A pivot on a radius of up to half a wingspan costs one point, up to a wingspan two to three points, and a larger radius four or five, with a wing-over zeroed.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft's centre of gravity moves sideways, in the direction the aircraft turns, from the start of the stall turn. Movement caused by drifting downwind with the wind is removed, but drift upwind is not. The largest width beyond a 2 m allowance is charged once. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it is an approximation of the wingspan-based rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the sideways distance moved in metres with the 2 m allowance as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement up to the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced width that is charged.

> The model aircraft comes to a stop in forward movement and then must pivot around its centre of gravity (CG) in the yaw axis for the manoeuvre to receive a high score. If the model aircraft does not pivot on the CG, but within a radius of a half-wingspan, 1 point is subtracted. For a radius of pivot up to one wingspan, 2 to 3 points are subtracted and if the radius exceeds 1½ wingspans, the manoeuvre must be downgraded 4 to 5 points.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

> Drift of the model aircraft during the stalled condition must be ignored, provided the model aircraft does not drift outside the manoeuvring zone.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.drift)

### Stall Turn Height Loss {#height}

`height`

Checks that the aircraft does not lose height through the pivot of a stall turn. How far below its highest point the aircraft is at the start and end of the stall turn, beyond 2 m, is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The aircraft should stop, pivot about its centre of gravity and then descend, not slide backwards or drop through the pivot. An aircraft that flops forward or backwards is zeroed, and a pivot well away from the centre of gravity is downgraded.

    FCScore measures how far below the highest point of the stall turn the aircraft is at the first and last points of the stall turn element. Any height lost beyond a 2 m allowance is charged. The rulebook does not give a height allowance; this is an FCScore approximation of a clean pivot.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows how far the aircraft is below its highest point, in metres, with the 2 m allowance as dashed lines. The judged line follows the measurement inside the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced height loss that is charged.

> The model aircraft comes to a stop in forward movement and then must pivot around its centre of gravity (CG) in the yaw axis for the manoeuvre to receive a high score. If the model aircraft does not pivot on the CG, but within a radius of a half-wingspan, 1 point is subtracted. For a radius of pivot up to one wingspan, 2 to 3 points are subtracted and if the radius exceeds 1½ wingspans, the manoeuvre must be downgraded 4 to 5 points.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

> If the model aircraft flops forward or backward in a stall turn, a zero score must be given. If the model aircraft shows a pendulum movement after the pivot, the manoeuvre is downgraded by 1 point.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.exit)

### Stall Turn Exit Movement {#exit_groundspeed}

`exit_groundspeed`

Checks that the aircraft has no horizontal movement along its nose direction at the end of the stall turn. The size of that movement is charged once. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the pivot the aircraft should be on a vertical downline, with no forward or backward flop or pendulum movement and no skid.

    FCScore takes the last point of the stall turn and measures the horizontal speed over the ground of the aircraft along its nose direction, charging its absolute value. A larger movement means the aircraft has left the pivot travelling sideways or forwards instead of straight down.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> If the model aircraft flops forward or backward in a stall turn, a zero score must be given. If the model aircraft shows a pendulum movement after the pivot, the manoeuvre is downgraded by 1 point.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.exit)

### Pitch Into Stall Turn {#prestallturn_pitch}

`prestallturn_pitch`

Checks the pitch of the up-line into a stall turn, using the flight path first and the nose attitude close to the top. Only growth in the error is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    The lines of a stall turn must have exactly vertical flight paths. Near the top the aircraft slows to a stop and wind correction is no longer expected in the stalled condition, so the line is judged first on where it is going and, as it stops, on how it is pointing.

    FCScore divides the line into a part judged on flight path and a final part judged on nose attitude, and chooses the changeover point that gives the smallest downgrade. Within each part it charges each increase in the absolute pitch error and not decreases. The attitude part means a stalled aircraft is not charged for flight path wander at the top. The scale is calibrated to the F3A rule of about one point per 15° of deviation.

    Because every separate increase is charged, small wobbles add up with time, so the same flying in a bigger manoeuvre, which takes longer at the same speed, would collect more of them. To keep the size of the manoeuvre from counting against the pilot, this downgrade is multiplied by (reference duration / flown duration) to the power 0.75, limited to between 0.7 and 1.4. The reference duration is the time the manoeuvre takes at the size in its definition, without the entry and exit lines, and the flown duration is the same span in the flight, so a manoeuvre flown about 10% bigger is charged about 7% less for each error.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The criteria in this manoeuvre are mainly about lines. The lines must have exactly vertical and horizontal flight paths.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.lines)

> All manoeuvres are required to be wind corrected in such a way that the shape of the manoeuvre, as described in Annex 5A, is preserved in the model aircraft's flight path. The exceptions to this criterion are in the snap-rolls, stall turns, and spins, where the model aircraft is in a stalled condition.
>
> [5B.7](#rb-general.wind_correction)

`prestallturn_yaw`

Checks the sideways direction of the up-line into a stall turn, using the flight path first and the nose attitude close to the top. Only growth in the error is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The criteria in this manoeuvre are mainly about lines. The lines must have exactly vertical and horizontal flight paths.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.lines)

> All manoeuvres are required to be wind corrected in such a way that the shape of the manoeuvre, as described in Annex 5A, is preserved in the model aircraft's flight path. The exceptions to this criterion are in the snap-rolls, stall turns, and spins, where the model aircraft is in a stalled condition.

Checks the pitch of the down-line after a stall turn, using the nose attitude first and the flight path once the aircraft is moving. Only growth in the error is charged.     The lines of a stall turn must have exactly vertical flight paths. Just after the pivot the aircraft is still stalled and moving slowly, so the line is judged first on how it is pointing and, once it has picked up speed, on where it is going.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The criteria in this manoeuvre are mainly about lines. The lines must have exactly vertical and horizontal flight paths.
>
> [5B.8.11](#rb-stall_turns.lines)

> Drift of the model aircraft during the stalled condition must be ignored, provided the model aircraft does not drift outside the manoeuvring zone.
>
