## Positioning (box) downgrades

### Top Height Limit {#top}

`top`

Checks that the manoeuvre stays below the top of the manoeuvring zone. The angle above the height limit, averaged over the duration of the manoeuvre, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Errors are discounted for aircraft high in the box, where the limit is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    The manoeuvring zone has a height limit that rises as the flight line moves out, roughly 260 m high at 150 m and about 303 m at 175 m, which corresponds to a 60° elevation line from the pilot. A manoeuvre that violates the height should be downgraded by a point, more if the violation is severe.

    FCScore measures the elevation angle of the aircraft above the 60° line for the whole manoeuvre. Each stretch above the limit is charged in proportion to how far above it is and for how large a share of the manoeuvre's duration. It is an angle rather than a height, so the allowance grows with distance. The amount per point of error is an FCScore scale, not the rulebook's fixed one-point step.

    Visibility is based on the lateral and vertical position of the aircraft: errors are easier to judge when the aircraft is low and close to the box markers and harder when it is high, so small excursions high in the box are discounted. Large excursions are counted in full.

> The height of the manoeuvring zone increases as the flight line moves from its centre. At a distance of 150 meters the height is approximately 260 meters high. At a distance of 175 meters the height is approximately 303 meters. When the height of the manoeuvring zone is violated, a manoeuvre must be downgraded by 1 point. If the height of a manoeuvre is severely violated, a downgrade must be more severe (in the order of 2 to 3 points).
>
> [5B.10](#rb-positioning.height)

### Right 60° Line {#right}

`right`

Checks that the manoeuvre stays inside the 60° line on the right of the pilot. The angle beyond the line, averaged over the duration of the manoeuvre, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Errors are discounted for aircraft high in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The manoeuvring zone is bounded on each side by a 60° line from the pilot. Flying a manoeuvre partly out of the zone is downgraded in proportion to how much of the manoeuvre is outside, for example one point for about 10% of the manoeuvre past the line, and more as the proportion grows.

    FCScore measures the angle of the aircraft beyond the right-hand 60° line for the whole manoeuvre. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far past the line it is and for how large a share of the manoeuvre's duration, matching the idea that the penalty follows the proportion of the manoeuvre outside the zone. The amount per point of error is an FCScore scale rather than the rulebook's example figures.

    Visibility is based on the lateral and vertical position of the aircraft: it is easier to see the aircraft cross the line when it is low and close to the box markers and harder when it is high, so small excursions high in the box are discounted. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Downgrades for flying a manoeuvre partially out of the zone should be in proportion to the degree of infraction, ie a small part of the manoeuvre (10%) flown past a 60 degree line would call for a downgrade of 1 point, while more of the manoeuvre (30%, 40%, 50% …) flown past a 60 degree line must be downgraded accordingly by 3, 4, 5… points.
>
> [5B.12](#rb-positioning.zone_proportion)

### Left 60° Line {#left}

`left`

Checks that the manoeuvre stays inside the 60° line on the left of the pilot. The angle beyond the line, averaged over the duration of the manoeuvre, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Errors are discounted for aircraft high in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The manoeuvring zone is bounded on each side by a 60° line from the pilot. Flying a manoeuvre partly out of the zone is downgraded in proportion to how much of the manoeuvre is outside, for example one point for about 10% of the manoeuvre past the line, and more as the proportion grows.

    FCScore measures the angle of the aircraft beyond the left-hand 60° line for the whole manoeuvre. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far past the line it is and for how large a share of the manoeuvre's duration, matching the idea that the penalty follows the proportion of the manoeuvre outside the zone. The amount per point of error is an FCScore scale rather than the rulebook's example figures.

    Visibility is based on the lateral and vertical position of the aircraft: it is easier to see the aircraft cross the line when it is low and close to the box markers and harder when it is high, so small excursions high in the box are discounted. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Downgrades for flying a manoeuvre partially out of the zone should be in proportion to the degree of infraction, ie a small part of the manoeuvre (10%) flown past a 60 degree line would call for a downgrade of 1 point, while more of the manoeuvre (30%, 40%, 50% …) flown past a 60 degree line must be downgraded accordingly by 3, 4, 5… points.
>
> [5B.12](#rb-positioning.zone_proportion)

### Back Distance Limit {#back}

`back`

Checks that the manoeuvre is not flown too far from the pilot. The distance beyond the back limit, averaged over the duration of the manoeuvre, is charged, with drift during spins allowed for. Errors are discounted when the aircraft's drift direction is hard to see.

??? note "Details"

    Flying so far out that a manoeuvre is hard to evaluate should be downgraded: a flight line beyond about 175 m from the pilot costs at least a point, and beyond about 200 m more severely, because visibility is the main criterion. The drift of a spin while stalled is not a fault provided the aircraft stays in the zone.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is beyond the back limit of the box, 175 m from the pilot, over the whole manoeuvre. Each stretch beyond is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the manoeuvre's duration. Drift backwards during a spin is added back so it is not counted against the manoeuvre. The scale of the downgrade per metre is an FCScore scale.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: a depth error is hardest to see when the aircraft is straight in front of the judge, because the error then lies along the line of sight, and easier when the aircraft is off to one side, so small excursions straight ahead are discounted. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the distance from the pilot with spin drift removed, which is the value that is judged, with the 175 m limit as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement inside the limit and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced distance that is charged.

> Flying so far out as to make evaluation of a manoeuvre difficult should be severely downgraded. The main criterion here is visibility. For a large, highly visible model aircraft, a line of flight approximately 175m in front of the pilot may be appropriate, while a smaller less visible model aircraft might have to be flown at say 140 to 150m. Manoeuvres performed on a line greater than approximately 175m in front of the pilot must be downgraded by at least 1 point.
>
> [5B.10](#rb-positioning.distance)

### Centre Position {#centre}

`centre`

Checks that centre manoeuvres are centred on the centre flag. The angle between the centre point of the manoeuvre and the centre line is charged once for each centre point, and twice for a centred rolling loop (once for the loop, once for the roll). Errors are discounted for aircraft high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A centre manoeuvre must be flown so that it is centred on the centre line, and the downgrade for an off-centre manoeuvre follows the misplacement, from 0.5 to 4 points.

    FCScore measures the angle from the pilot between the aircraft and the centre line at the centre point of the manoeuvre defined by the figure. Where the centre falls between two elements it is the point where one ends and the next begins. Where it falls within a roll or loop it is found from the aircraft's attitude and flight path rather than from the time taken, since the roll rate and the rate of turn are not always constant: half way through a full roll is the point where the aircraft is inverted, and the middle of a half loop from vertical up to vertical down is the point where the flight path is horizontal. A centred rolling loop has two centre points, one where the loop's flight path reaches the middle of the loop and one where the roll reaches its middle, and each is charged. Other centred elements use the point half way along the flown path. The absolute angle is charged, so being off-centre in either direction costs the same, and manoeuvres that have no centre point are not charged.

    Visibility is based on the aircraft's position in the box: the weighting falls for aircraft high in the box or far off to one side, so small offsets there are discounted. Large offsets are counted in full.

> A centre manoeuvre must be flown so that it is centred on the centre line indicated by the centre flag. If the manoeuvre is flown off-centre, it must be downgraded according to the misplacement. This may be in the range of 0.5 to 4 points subtracted.
>
> [5B.10](#rb-positioning.centre)

## Inter-element downgrades

### Loop Radius Matching {#inter.loop_radius}

`inter.loop_radius`

Checks that the loops and part-loops in a manoeuvre that should have the same radius do match. Each radius is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Loops and part-loops within a manoeuvre must have the same radius. A minor difference costs 0.5 point and a severe one a point or more, each time it occurs. The first radius does not define the others, but it is the starting point: the judge compares each radius with the last one flown.

    FCScore takes the radius of each loop that the manoeuvre requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times larger one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the size. This compares different loops with each other; whether each loop is round is judged by Loop Roundness.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Loops and part-loops within one manoeuvre must have the same radius. Each occurrence of a minor difference in radius must downgrade the manoeuvre by 0.5 point, while more severe deviations may downgrade it by 1, 1.5, 2 or more points for each occurrence.
>
> [5B.8.4](#rb-loops.radius)

### Line Length Matching {#inter.line_length}

`inter.line_length`

Checks that lines that should be of equal length in a manoeuvre are. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    The length of a line is only graded when a manoeuvre has more than one line in a defined relationship to another, as in a square loop. A minor deviation costs 0.5 point and larger deviations more.

    FCScore takes the length of each line that the manoeuvre requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. This includes the lengths of the lines before and after a roll when they are required to be equal.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The length of a line should only be graded when a manoeuvre contains more than one line with a given relationship to each other ie as in a square loop. If there is a minor deviation in the relationship then 0.5 point is subtracted, and more points are subtracted for greater deviations.
>
> [5B.8.3](#rb-lines.geometry)

### Part-Roll Line Matching {#inter.point_length}

`inter.point_length`

Checks that the lines between consecutive part-rolls are of equal length. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Lines between consecutive part-rolls must be short and of equal length, so the rolls should be evenly spaced with the same short pause between each.

    FCScore takes the length flown in each of the pauses between consecutive part-rolls and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Lines between consecutive part-rolls must be short and of equal length.
>
> [5B.8.5 e)](#rb-lines.part_roll_spacing)

### Part-Roll Rate Matching {#inter.partial_roll_rate}

`inter.partial_roll_rate`

Checks that part-rolls in the same manoeuvre are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a manoeuvre with more than one part-roll, the part-rolls must have the same roll rate. The first part-roll does not define the rate, but it is the starting point: the judge compares each part-roll with the last one. Part-rolls and continuous rolls are considered separately, and integrated rolls are exempt.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each part-roll that the manoeuvre requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate, and a roll in the opposite direction is treated as a large mismatch. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> In all manoeuvres which have more than one continuous roll, the continuous rolls must have the same roll-rate. In all manoeuvres which have more than one part-roll, the part-rolls must have the same roll rate.
>
> [5B.8.5 d)](#rb-rolls.matching_rates)

### Continuous Roll Rate Matching {#inter.full_roll_rate}

`inter.full_roll_rate`

Checks that continuous rolls in the same manoeuvre are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a manoeuvre with more than one continuous roll, the continuous rolls must have the same roll rate. The first roll does not define the rate, but it is the starting point: the judge compares each roll with the last one. Continuous rolls and part-rolls are considered separately, and integrated rolls are exempt.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each continuous roll that the manoeuvre requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate, and a roll in the opposite direction is treated as a large mismatch. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> In all manoeuvres which have more than one continuous roll, the continuous rolls must have the same roll-rate. In all manoeuvres which have more than one part-roll, the part-rolls must have the same roll rate.
>
> [5B.8.5 d)](#rb-rolls.matching_rates)

### Snap Rate Matching {#inter.snap_rate}

`inter.snap_rate`

Checks that snaps in the same manoeuvre are flown at the same rotation rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    F3A does not state that the rotation rates of snap-rolls must match, so this applies the roll-rate matching principle to snaps as an FCScore interpretation, not an explicit rule.

    FCScore takes the rotation rate of each snap that the manoeuvre requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

### Roll Position On Line {#inter.pad_length}

`inter.pad_length`

Checks that a roll is centred on its line, with equal lengths of line before and after it. The two lengths are compared and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Whenever a roll, part-roll, snap or combination of these is placed on a line, the lengths of line before and after must be equal. A minor difference costs 0.5 point, a major one a point or more, and the complete absence of a line before or after the roll costs 3 points.

    FCScore compares the length of line before the roll with the length after, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A roll that is perfectly centred scores zero, whatever the length of the line.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Whenever a continuous roll, part-roll, snap roll, or a consecutive combination of these is placed on a line, the length of the line before and after the roll or the combination of consecutive rolls must be equal. 0.5 point is subtracted for a minor difference, and 1 or more points for a major difference. If there is a complete absence of a line before or after the roll, 3 points are subtracted.
>
> [5B.8.10](#rb-lines.roll_placement)

## Rulebook references

### 5B.10 {#rb-positioning.centre}

`positioning.centre`

> A centre manoeuvre must be flown so that it is centred on the centre line indicated by the centre flag. If the manoeuvre is flown off-centre, it must be downgraded according to the misplacement. This may be in the range of 0.5 to 4 points subtracted.

### 5B.10 {#rb-positioning.distance}

`positioning.distance`

> Flying so far out as to make evaluation of a manoeuvre difficult should be severely downgraded. The main criterion here is visibility. For a large, highly visible model aircraft, a line of flight approximately 175m in front of the pilot may be appropriate, while a smaller less visible model aircraft might have to be flown at say 140 to 150m. Manoeuvres performed on a line greater than approximately 175m in front of the pilot must be downgraded by at least 1 point.

### 5B.10 {#rb-positioning.height}

`positioning.height`

> The height of the manoeuvring zone increases as the flight line moves from its centre. At a distance of 150 meters the height is approximately 260 meters high. At a distance of 175 meters the height is approximately 303 meters. When the height of the manoeuvring zone is violated, a manoeuvre must be downgraded by 1 point. If the height of a manoeuvre is severely violated, a downgrade must be more severe (in the order of 2 to 3 points).

### 5B.11 {#rb-size}

`size`

> The size of a manoeuvre is defined by its matching size relative to the size of the manoeuvring zone and relative to the size of the other manoeuvres performed throughout a schedule. For not matching size up to 1 point downgrade.

### 5B.12 {#rb-positioning.zone_proportion}

`positioning.zone_proportion`

> Downgrades for flying a manoeuvre partially out of the zone should be in proportion to the degree of infraction, ie a small part of the manoeuvre (10%) flown past a 60 degree line would call for a downgrade of 1 point, while more of the manoeuvre (30%, 40%, 50% …) flown past a 60 degree line must be downgraded accordingly by 3, 4, 5… points.

### 5B.2 {#rb-lines.level_flight}

`lines.level_flight`

> The flight path of a model aircraft is used to judge the shape of all manoeuvres, and manoeuvres must be entered and exited with straight and level upright or inverted flight of recognisable length.

### 5B.3 {#rb-speed.ground_speed}

`speed.ground_speed`

> Constant Flying Speed (three-dimensional velocity—not airspeed);

### 5B.5 {#rb-general.downgrading}

`general.downgrading`

> Every manoeuvre starts with the mark of 10 points and will be downgraded for each defect during the execution of the manoeuvre in one or multiple 0.5 point steps, depending on the severity of the defect.

### 5B.6 {#rb-general.flight_path}

`general.flight_path`

> The flight path of a model aircraft is the trajectory of its centre of gravity. The attitude is the direction of the fuselage centre-line in relation to the flight path. If not otherwise stated, all judging is based on flight path.

### 5B.7 {#rb-general.wind_correction}

`general.wind_correction`

> All manoeuvres are required to be wind corrected in such a way that the shape of the manoeuvre, as described in Annex 5A, is preserved in the model aircraft's flight path. The exceptions to this criterion are in the snap-rolls, stall turns, and spins, where the model aircraft is in a stalled condition.

### 5B.8.1 {#rb-general.geometry}

`general.geometry`

> As a guide for downgrading deviations from the defined manoeuvre geometry, the manoeuvres are divided into their different components: lines, loops, rolls, snap-rolls, horizontal circles, line/loop/roll/horizontal circle combinations, stall turns, and spins.

### 5B.8.10 {#rb-lines.roll_placement}

`lines.roll_placement`

> Whenever a continuous roll, part-roll, snap roll, or a consecutive combination of these is placed on a line, the length of the line before and after the roll or the combination of consecutive rolls must be equal. 0.5 point is subtracted for a minor difference, and 1 or more points for a major difference. If there is a complete absence of a line before or after the roll, 3 points are subtracted.

### 5B.8.10 {#rb-rolls.integration}

`rolls.integration`

> Flight paths of continuous rolls or part-rolls that are integrated with loops or horizontal circles should be smooth, continuous, and of constant radius. Where an integrated roll is required, quick-rolling should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.11 {#rb-stall_turns.drift}

`stall_turns.drift`

> Drift of the model aircraft during the stalled condition must be ignored, provided the model aircraft does not drift outside the manoeuvring zone.

### 5B.8.11 {#rb-stall_turns.exit}

`stall_turns.exit`

> If the model aircraft flops forward or backward in a stall turn, a zero score must be given. If the model aircraft shows a pendulum movement after the pivot, the manoeuvre is downgraded by 1 point.

### 5B.8.11 {#rb-stall_turns.lines}

`stall_turns.lines`

> The criteria in this manoeuvre are mainly about lines. The lines must have exactly vertical and horizontal flight paths.

### 5B.8.11 {#rb-stall_turns.pivot}

`stall_turns.pivot`

> The model aircraft comes to a stop in forward movement and then must pivot around its centre of gravity (CG) in the yaw axis for the manoeuvre to receive a high score. If the model aircraft does not pivot on the CG, but within a radius of a half-wingspan, 1 point is subtracted. For a radius of pivot up to one wingspan, 2 to 3 points are subtracted and if the radius exceeds 1½ wingspans, the manoeuvre must be downgraded 4 to 5 points.

### 5B.8.11 {#rb-stall_turns.torque_off}

`stall_turns.torque_off`

> If the model aircraft should “torque-off” during the stall turn, a downgrade must be applied using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.entry}

`spins.entry`

> The entry is flown in a horizontal flight path with the nose-up attitude increasing as the speed decreases. Drift of the model aircraft from the flight path at this point should not be downgraded, since it is in a near-stalled condition. However, severe yawing during the near-stalled condition, should be downgraded by 1 point per 15 degrees. A climbing flight path just prior to the spin must be downgraded, using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.exit}

`spins.exit`

> A vertical downward line of visible length must be held after the rotation stops. The pull- or push-out is judged like a part-loop and if followed by a part-roll, should be separated by a well-defined line of straight flight.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.rotation}

`spins.rotation`

> Different models spin in different attitudes, and the attitude is not to be taken into consideration, as long as the model aircraft is stalled. Any reversals in direction must be immediate, and if the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the spin, the manoeuvre is severely downgraded.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.slide_in}

`spins.slide_in`

> If the model aircraft slides into the spin (is loath to spin), the manoeuvre must be downgraded by using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.stall_break}

`spins.stall_break`

> The nose then drops as the model aircraft stalls. Simultaneously as the nose drops, the wing also drops in the direction of the spin.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.stalled}

`spins.stalled`

> If the model aircraft does not stall or if the model aircraft is snap-rolled or spiral-dived into the spin, the manoeuvre is zeroed.

### 5B.8.12 {#rb-spins.stop}

`spins.stop`

> After the defined number of turns, the stop of rotation is judged in the same manner as for a roll, downgraded 1 point per 15 degree deviation of heading. The spin rotation should stop parallel to the flight line. “Unloading”, or stopping the spin rotation early and then applying only aileron to roll the model aircraft to the desired attitude, should be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.2 {#rb-general.fifteen_degrees}

`general.fifteen_degrees`

> 1 point must be subtracted for each approximate 15 degrees deviation, but 0.5 points only for half of this. In general, lines must be judged more critically than deviations in yaw or roll.

### 5B.8.3 {#rb-lines.geometry}

`lines.geometry`

> The length of a line should only be graded when a manoeuvre contains more than one line with a given relationship to each other ie as in a square loop. If there is a minor deviation in the relationship then 0.5 point is subtracted, and more points are subtracted for greater deviations.

### 5B.8.4 {#rb-loops.definition}

`loops.definition`

> A loop must have by definition, a constant radius, and must be performed in the vertical plane throughout. It is entered and exited by a well-defined line which, for a complete loop, is horizontal. For a part-loop, however, such lines may be in any other plane of flight as required by the particular manoeuvre.

### 5B.8.4 {#rb-loops.plane}

`loops.plane`

> If the loop is not performed entirely in the vertical plane ie it drifts closer or further from the judges, minor drift must be downgraded by 0.5 point, while more severe drift must be downgraded more.

### 5B.8.4 {#rb-loops.radius}

`loops.radius`

> Loops and part-loops within one manoeuvre must have the same radius. Each occurrence of a minor difference in radius must downgrade the manoeuvre by 0.5 point, while more severe deviations may downgrade it by 1, 1.5, 2 or more points for each occurrence.

### 5B.8.4 {#rb-loops.segmentation}

`loops.segmentation`

> Every loop or part-loop must be performed without interruption to the circular flight path. Every segmentation must be downgraded by 0.5 or more points.

### 5B.8.5 a) {#rb-rolls.constant_path}

`rolls.constant_path`

> They must be performed on a constant flight path.

### 5B.8.5 b) {#rb-rolls.rate}

`rolls.rate`

> The roll-rate must be constant. Minor variations in roll-rate must be downgraded by 0.5 point, while more severe variations must receive a downgrade of 1 or more points. Slowing down (or speeding up) the roll-rate towards the end of a roll must be downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.8.5 c) {#rb-rolls.start_stop}

`rolls.start_stop`

> The start and stop of the rotation must be crisp and well-defined. If a start or stop is badly defined, 0.5 or more points are to be subtracted for each.

### 5B.8.5 d) {#rb-rolls.matching_rates}

`rolls.matching_rates`

> In all manoeuvres which have more than one continuous roll, the continuous rolls must have the same roll-rate. In all manoeuvres which have more than one part-roll, the part-rolls must have the same roll rate.

### 5B.8.5 e) {#rb-lines.part_roll_spacing}

`lines.part_roll_spacing`

> Lines between consecutive part-rolls must be short and of equal length.

### 5B.8.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.axial_disguise}

`snap_rolls.axial_disguise`

> If the stall-break does not occur and the model aircraft barrel-rolls around, the manoeuvre must be severely downgraded (more than 5 points). Similarly, axial rolls disguised as snap-rolls must be severely downgraded (more than 5 points).

### 5B.8.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.definition}

`snap_rolls.definition`

> A snap-roll is a rapid auto-rotative roll where the model aircraft is in a stalled attitude, with a continuous high angle of attack.

### 5B.8.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.geometry}

`snap_rolls.geometry`

> Snap-rolls are judged in the same way as axial rolls as far as the constant flight path throughout the snap-roll, the start and stop of the rotation, and the roll direction is concerned.

### 5B.8.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.stall_break}

`snap_rolls.stall_break`

> At the start of a snap-roll, the fuselage attitude must show a definite stall-break and attitude separation from the flight path, before the rotation is started, since the model aircraft is supposed to be in a stalled condition throughout the snap-roll.

### 5B.8.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.unstalled}

`snap_rolls.unstalled`

> If the model aircraft returns to an unstalled condition during the snap-roll, the manoeuvre is downgraded using the 1 point per 15 degree rule.

### 5B.9 {#rb-speed}

`speed`

> The model aircraft shall maintain a constant flight speed throughout the various manoeuvre components; for example, in climbing and descending sections. For significant differences up to one point is subtracted.
